properties.decision:
DECIDED on Anthony's word, 2026-09-16 ("go with diff-driven impact idea first"), when he asked whether his brother's cross-project and git-linking idea had ever been followed up. Built as tools/impact_of_diff.py — wiring, no core change, the core still does no file I/O: the driver lists the range's files with git, hashes the ones a registered Artifact points at (by exact `location` or by a parent-directory artifact), calls reconcile_artifacts for the propagation seeds and propagate_from for the radius, and prints the capabilities and requirements reached. The design question the idea named is settled the loud way: unmapped files are reported FIRST and counted, never folded into a clean result, and `--fail-on-unmapped` makes them an exit code only for a gate that opts in, so the read never punishes a project that has not finished registering (dec:idea-allocation-waits-for-the-last-responsible-moment). The export document itself is set aside as record rather than build. First run on the real repository, the #519 merge: 12 files mapped, 4 named as invisible (an integration test and three tool snapshots), 9 requirements reached directly. Pinned by tools/test_impact_of_diff.py, six cases, in CI. The text below is the brainstorm as it was recorded and stays as history.

═══ AS RECORDED 2026-08-05 ═══
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Source: Alex Sligar's 2026-08-05 research, specifically Understand Anything's "diff impact analysis that shows what a given change touches".

THE IDEA: reflow2's impact analysis runs design-first — add_change_event then propagate_change, seeded by the design node you are about to touch. The survey's tools run it code-first: here is a diff, here is what it touches. Those are opposite directions, and the code-first direction is the one a developer actually has in hand at review time.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, and this was checked rather than assumed: reconcile_artifacts takes observed artifact hashes and returns `propagation_seeds` — "the design nodes the changes land on" — explicitly documented to be fed to propagate_from. So the code-to-design hop is BUILT. The composition is: changed files, to registered artifacts by hash, to REALIZES edges, to capabilities and upward. Nothing is missing in the core.

WHAT WAS THEREFORE ACTUALLY OPEN, and it was smaller than the survey made it sound: (a) nothing computed the hashes from a commit; (b) the CI gate checks the committed export for drift and open gaps, not "what does this commit touch upstream"; (c) the answer is only as complete as artifact registration, and an unregistered file lands on nothing at all, which would read as "this change is safe" rather than "this change is unmapped". That last one was the real risk and it is the same failure mode as the release-manifest problem: silence that looks like a pass.

THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, which shaped the build: a per-commit blast radius is only as trustworthy as REALIZES coverage, and an incomplete golden thread turns it into a confident understatement — worse than no answer, because a reviewer will believe it. The built version reports unmapped files as UNMAPPED and loudly. The existing unrealized_capability gap is the design-side half of that problem; this driver is the artifact-side half.
properties.name: DECIDED 2026-09-16 — a git diff is a direct input to impact analysis: tools/impact_of_diff.py drives reconcile_artifacts then propagate_from from a commit range, and names every changed file the design cannot see
properties.rationale: Recorded as an idea rather than a gap because the machinery it asks for already exists and only the driver is absent, which makes it a small increment rather than a design question — except for the unmapped-file silence, which is a design question and is the reason this is worth a node at all.
